query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Real‐time adaptive laser power modulation during additive manufacturing will improve the dimensional precision and mechanical integrity of high‐entropy alloy components by reducing thermal gradients that cause pore formation and microstructural inhomogeneity.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐fabricated high‐entropy alloy components (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi or similar compositions) produced using standard constant laser power processes that exhibit dimensional deviations, undesirable residual stresses, and fabrication-induced defects such as porosity.
generation.intervention: Implementation of a real‐time feedback control system that modulates the laser power during directed energy deposition (or laser powder bed fusion) based on in-situ temperature and melt pool monitoring.
generation.conditions: Under standard inert gas atmosphere and typical scanning speeds used in directed energy deposition of high‐entropy alloys; applying the intervention to components with similar compositions (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi systems) and geometry as studied in recent laser cladding and ML-based parameter optimization experiments.
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform and controlled melt pool, resulting in decreased peak temperatures and thermal gradients, which in turn refine the microstructure, reduce porosity, and improve grain homogeneity.
generation.mechanism: Adaptive laser power modulation minimizes thermal overshoots and rapid cooling during deposition, thereby reducing residual stresses and inhibiting defect nucleation. This leads to a more uniform microstructure and better bonding between layers, which enhances both dimensional accuracy and mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the current fabrication baseline using fixed laser parameters, specimens manufactured with adaptive laser power control are expected to show a measurable reduction in dimensional deviation, lower defect density (e.g., fewer pores), and improved mechanical performance (higher yield strength and ductility).
generation.baseline: High‐entropy alloy components produced with constant laser power settings and a fixed scanning path that yield inconsistent melt pool dynamics leading to higher defect concentrations and dimensional inaccuracies.
generation.boundary: This effect is anticipated under typical DED or laser powder bed fusion conditions for alloys similar to AlCoCrFeNi; the benefit may vary for different HEA compositions, extreme processing conditions, or when other variables (such as powder feed rate or ambient temperature) become dominant factors.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvements in dimensional precision and mechanical integrity remains uncertain and may depend on the specific alloy composition and the sensitivity and response time of the feedback control system. Further, integration challenges in different AM systems could influence the outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high‐entropy alloy specimens using a directed energy deposition system under identical environmental conditions and processing parameters except for the laser control strategy. One set (control group) will use a constant laser power setting, while the other (experimental group) will use a real‐time adaptive laser power modulation scheme. In-situ sensors will record melt pool temperature profiles and dynamics. After fabrication, use high-resolution 3D scanning and X-ray computed tomography to assess dimensional accuracy and defect density, respectively; perform standard tensile tests to evaluate mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility).
measurements: Defect (porosity) density via X-ray computed tomography
Mechanical properties (yield strength and elongation) via tensile testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental group does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision (lower deviations), reduced defect density, and enhanced mechanical properties compared to the control group, the hypothesis that adaptive laser power modulation improves the performance of additively manufactured high-entropy alloys will be falsified.

Material-agnostic machine learning approach enables high relative density in powder bed fusion products

Abstract: This study introduces a method that is applicable across various powder materials to predict process conditions that yield a product with a relative density greater than 98% by laser powder bed fusion. We develop an XGBoost model using a dataset comprising material properties of powder and process conditions, and its output, relative density, undergoes a transformation using a sigmoid function to increase accuracy. We deeply examine the relationships between input features and the target value using Shapley additive explanations. Experimental validation with stainless steel 316 L, AlSi10Mg, and Fe60Co15Ni15Cr10 medium entropy alloy powders verifies the method’s reproducibility and transferability. This research contributes to laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing by offering a universally applicable strategy to optimize process conditions. Process Parameters Optimization and Numerical Simulation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Coating via Laser Cladding

Abstract: The use of laser cladding technology to prepare coatings of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy holds enormous potential for application. However, the cladding quality will have a considerable effect on the properties of the coatings. In this study, considering the complex coupling relationship between cladding quality and the process parameters, an orthogonal experimental design was employed, with laser power, scanning speed, and powder feed rate as correlation factor variables, and microhardness, dilution rate, and aspect ratio as characteristic variables. The experimental data underwent gray correlation analysis to determine the effect of various process parameters on the quality of cladding. Then, the NSGA-II algorithm was used to establish a multi-objective optimization model of process parameters. Finally, the ANSYS Workbench simulation model was employed to conduct numerical simulations on a group of optimized process parameters and analyze the change rule of the temperature field.
